title: What Not to Put in Your Family Emergency Binder
description: Nearly every emergency binder checklist tells you to include Social Security cards, card images and passwords. That advice assumes a locked safe. If your binder is meant to be found in a hurry, here is what belongs in it and what does not.
answer: Keep the map in the binder and the keys somewhere else. A binder is meant to be found fast, so it should hold contacts, locations and instructions, not Social Security cards, passwords, full account numbers or card images. Store those in a locked or fireproof place and record only where they are.
intro: Search for an emergency binder checklist and you will find the same list a dozen times over. Social Security cards for everyone in the house. Copies of every credit and debit card, front and back. Passports, birth certificates, account numbers, insurance policies, and a page of passwords. Then, usually near the end, one line: keep it somewhere your family can find it quickly.

Read those two instructions next to each other and the problem becomes obvious. You have been told to assemble the most complete identity kit anyone could hope to find, and then to make it easy to find.

The list is not wrong. Those documents genuinely matter in a disaster, and the federal guidance says so. What is missing is the distinction between the information you need to reach for in an emergency and the documents you need to protect from one. They are not the same set, they do not want the same storage, and collapsing them into a single binder is how a preparedness project turns into a liability.

sections.heading: The standard list is right. The standard container is not.
paragraphs: FEMA and Operation HOPE publish the Emergency Financial First Aid Kit, the closest thing to an official version of this exercise. It asks for household identification, financial and legal documents, medical information and contacts, and it is a genuinely good piece of work.

It also assumes something most blog checklists quietly drop: that you are safeguarding these documents, not merely gathering them. FEMA's companion sheet on protecting critical documents is explicit about storage — originals secured, copies kept separately, and a second copy somewhere outside the house.

Somewhere between the federal guidance and the tenth listicle, the safeguarding half falls off. What survives is the shopping list, plus the advice to keep it handy. That combination is the actual mistake, and almost nobody names it.

sections.heading: The thing that makes a binder work is the thing that makes it dangerous
paragraphs: An emergency binder earns its place by being findable. A neighbour arrives, a sitter needs the pediatrician, a relative has to reach your sister, you have ten minutes to leave. The whole value is that someone who does not know your house can put a hand on it.

That is also the specification for something worth stealing. The higher-value target in a burglary is no longer the television; it is a folder that consolidates identity documents for everyone who lives there. A binder labelled clearly, kept somewhere obvious, holding cards and numbers for four people, is the best forty seconds a thief will have all week.
So the binder has to be two things at once, and it cannot be. The resolution is not a better hiding place. It is to stop asking one object to do both jobs.

sections.heading: What does not belong in a findable binder
paragraphs: None of these are useless. Every one of them matters at some point. They simply do not belong in the object designed to be located quickly by someone who is not you.
bullets: Social Security cards, or the numbers written out. The Social Security Administration's guidance is to keep the card secure rather than carry it, and a binder on a shelf is closer to carrying it than to securing it. Almost nothing you do in the first hours of an emergency requires the number.

Photocopies of credit and debit cards, front and back. The back is the security code. A card image is a card. If you want a record of what is in your wallet, write down the issuer and the number to call — that is what you actually need when the wallet is gone.

Passwords, PINs, and security question answers. A written password list has one job, and anyone who finds it can do that job. If you keep one, it belongs with your valuables, not with your instructions.

Full account numbers. The institution, the branch, the phone number and whose name is on it will get a family member through any conversation they need to have. The last four digits are enough to identify the account to the person on the phone.
Original passports and birth certificates. These belong in whatever you would protect from a fire, not in something you can flip through. Note where they are instead.
Spare keys, safe combinations, and alarm codes. A binder that tells a stranger how to open everything else in the house has undone the rest of the house's security.

sections.heading: What belongs in it instead
paragraphs: What is left after that subtraction is not a thin document. It is most of what anyone actually needs, and it has the useful property of being harmless if it is seen by the wrong person.
This is the difference between a map and a set of keys. A map tells you where the safe is and who to call; keys open it. In an emergency, almost every question is a map question.
bullets: People, with the relationship spelled out. Not just a number — Dana, my sister, has a key and knows the children. Whoever arrives may not know who anyone is.
Where things live. The deed is in the grey box on the closet shelf. The will is with the attorney, and here is her name. This is the single highest-value page and it contains no secrets at all.
Medical essentials. Allergies, conditions, current medications and doses, the pediatrician, the pharmacy. This is the page that gets read out loud in an emergency room.
Children, pets, and the household. School and daycare, who may collect them, the vet, the feeding routine, where the water shut-off and the breaker panel are.
A ten-minute list. What to carry out and in what order, with the location of each item. Printed twice — one copy near the door, one in the car.
Insurance you can identify. Carrier, agent, policy type and the claims number. Enough to start a claim; not enough to impersonate you.

sections.heading: Where the documents themselves should go
paragraphs: Having removed the sensitive material, it needs somewhere to be. There is no perfect answer here, only a trade-off worth making deliberately.

A fireproof, waterproof safe bolted down at home keeps documents accessible and survives most household fires. It is the usual answer for birth certificates, passports, the deed and the policies. Note that many consumer safes are rated for paper but not for the plastic of a passport or a drive.

A safe deposit box is more secure and considerably less convenient. It is a poor place for anything anyone might need on a weekend, at night, or immediately after a death, because access can be restricted at exactly the moment the family needs it. It suits documents you must not lose and will rarely need, not the ones your executor needs on day one. If you are thinking through that longer horizon, getting your affairs in order covers what a family needs to be able to reach.

A copy somewhere else is the part people skip, and it is the part that matters after a fire. Whatever you decide, one set of copies should live outside the house — with a relative, in a deposit box, or on an encrypted drive you control. If a disaster has already happened, the first 72 hours after a fire or flood covers what to do in what order, and documenting your home before you need to prove it covers the record your insurer will ask for.

sections.heading: If the binder is already lost, or was stolen
paragraphs: Treat it as a breach rather than a lost object, and work in the order of what can be used fastest.

Call the card issuers first; a card image is usable within minutes and a replacement takes one phone call. Then place a fraud alert or a credit freeze with the three credit bureaus. A freeze is free, takes minutes, and is the single most effective step available to you.

If Social Security cards or numbers were in it, report it at the FTC's IdentityTheft.gov, which generates a recovery plan and the affidavit banks ask for. The Social Security Administration's own guidance is that a replacement card is rarely the useful step; monitoring and freezing credit is. Change any password that was written down, starting with the email account that can reset the others.
Then rebuild the binder as two objects rather than one, which is the version that should have existed the first time.

faq.q: Should I include copies of passports and birth certificates in an emergency binder?
faq.a: Keep the originals in a fireproof safe or safe deposit box and note their location in the binder. If you want copies for a disaster, store them with the originals or outside the house rather than in the binder someone is meant to find quickly. What the binder needs is the location and the document numbers, not the documents themselves.

faq.q: Is it safer to scan everything and keep it in the cloud instead?
faq.a: It solves the burglary problem and creates a different one. A cloud folder holding identity documents for a whole household is a valuable target and depends on one password holding. If you do it, use a separate strong password and two-factor authentication, and understand that you have moved the risk rather than removed it. Many people are better served by a locked box at home and a copy with a relative.

faq.q: Can I just keep the whole binder in a locked fireproof safe?
faq.a: You can, and it is safe, but then it is not an emergency binder. If a sitter or a neighbour cannot reach it, it will not do the job you built it for. That is the trade-off the two-object approach resolves: an unlocked page with the contacts and locations, and a locked box holding the documents it points to.

takeaway: An emergency binder is meant to be found, so build it as though it will be found by the wrong person. Keep contacts, locations, medical essentials and instructions in the part that stays reachable, and keep cards, numbers, passwords and originals in something that locks. Nothing in the reachable half should be dangerous in the wrong hands, which is also what makes it safe to leave on a fridge or hand to a sitter, and that is the whole point of having one.

productPitch: The Family Emergency Binder is this split already built. It records who to call, where things are, and what the children and animals need, and it never asks for a Social Security number, an account number or a password because there is nowhere in it to put one. It prints the fridge page, the sitter page and the ten-minute list — pages that are safe to leave where they can be found.
